The whole backend is one endpoint, /ws/odds, that sends RANDOM numbers for a placeholder "Team A vs Team B" every 3 seconds. It uses no odds API, no vendor, no scraper, no database and no real bookmaker data. Part 2 (the Angular client) is announced but I found no sign it was ever published. verdict.why: This is not an odds or scores source. It is a toy WebSocket demo that streams random numbers every 3 seconds, with no vendor, no upstream and no timestamp. It is free only because it has no data, so it cannot beat CNO or the Novig makers. The technique is a FastAPI WebSocket relay that fans a feed out to browsers (Angular). Vigilant is a single-user Android app that can open the upstream sockets or REST polls itself (Polymarket, Sofascore and so on), so a relay would only add a hop, a host and latency. The tutorial's timer loop also decouples send time from change time, the opposite of what the bar needs. Even if a real feed were swapped in, a viewer would see that feed's age plus up to 3 s. Nothing here needs further research and nothing here needs a phone test. The real question is which upstream to relay, and this article does not answer it.

result.what_it_is: A vendor advertisement written as a tutorial. It was published 2026-05-21T13:06:54Z (dateModified is identical) and I read it 2026-10-07. The byline is "E. Mitev". It argues for using an aggregator API instead of scraping Bet365, FanDuel and DraftKings, and it recommends and uses one vendor, PulseScore (pulsescore.net, api.pulsescore.net). The code is two short Python snippets. One polls pre-match odds over REST with an X-Secret header. The other prints frames from a WebSocket. The article is an ad. The author's DEV profile reads "We provide real-time sports odds from Bet365, Paddy Power & more via API ... Free tier available - no credit card needed", with website pulsescore.net and Twitter handle @pulsescoreapi. The account was created 2026-05-21, the same day as the post, and has 8 posts that all promote PulseScore. This post has no disclosure line, 0 reactions and 0 comments. A later post by the same account (2026-10-06) does say "Disclosure: We build PulseScore." The same vendor is probably behind other sources in this batch (items 8 and 10 point to pulsescore.net).
result.upstream_data_source: PulseScore's own scrapers of bookmakers' consumer sites. They write into a database (the stream doc says "seq is the Mongo cluster time"), and PulseScore serves that copy over REST, a per-bookmaker WebSocket and a delta-stream WebSocket. It is not a licensed feed and not a book's own socket. Evidence (all VERIFIED on the vendor's own pages): the homepage says "Live betting odds from soccer and tennis - scraped from top bookmakers and updated every second"; the PS3838 Swagger text says "The scraper rewrites every event it still tracks on each pass"; the vendor's blog post says "we thought we were building a collection of scrapers ... Most of the engineering effort went into reliability, normalization, monitoring". The Terms call the data "aggregated publicly available sports betting odds data" from "third-party bookmaker sources". The Kalshi and Polymarket entries are derived rather than copied. The Kalshi Swagger text says "decimal odds derived from the last traded price plus the current best bid/ask" (CLAIM_ONLY). The article's thesis is "stop scraping", but the product it sells is a scrape run by someone else. The vendor's own post lists endpoints disappearing and Cloudflare updates as a recurring problem, so the upstream can break without notice (INFERRED).
result.push_or_poll: There are three ways in. (1) REST polling: free BASIC is 500 requests a month at 1 request/s per bookmaker; the article's first snippet is this one. (2) A legacy per-bookmaker, per-sport WebSocket (wss://api.pulsescore.net/api/{bookmaker}/ws/live?key=..&sport=..) that pushes a frame about every second with every live event for that sport; PRO and above only. (3) A Stream API (Beta, protocol v2, wss://api.pulsescore.net/api/stream/ws) that sends one snapshot and then keyed deltas, batched once a second, with a seq number and a 120 s resume window; also PRO and above. The article's second snippet (the socket) cannot work on the free key the article tells readers to use. Pricing page, Terms and docs all put sockets on PRO and above. The docs say BASIC and STARTER handshakes are rejected with close code 4003.
result.claimed_latency_or_refresh: Marketing claims only. The article says "Live events update every 1 second" and "a 1-2 second refresh rate". The homepage says "refreshed every ~1 second". The stream page says "Every odds change, the moment it lands." The vendor's own stream doc is more modest: "Changes are batched once per second per stream, so a delta typically arrives 1-2 seconds after the bookmaker's write; this is not a sub-second feed." The October tutorial adds that the one-second cadence "is not a guarantee that every bookmaker price reaches your application within one second." It also says "We have not tested this wrapper against the authenticated live service. This tutorial does not report a live latency benchmark." A search snippet of the Product Hunt page (second-hand; Product Hunt returned 403 to the container) lists under-1-second live updates as a goal, not a result.
result.measured_or_verified_age:
None. I could not measure the age of any price or score. Reasons:
1. Every odds endpoint needs a key and returns 401 without one ({"message":"User is not authorized"}). I did not sign up, as the rules require.
2. The only keyless endpoint is /api/stream/capabilities, which lists bookmakers and sports. I probed it once. Its discoveredAt (23:31:40Z) was 7 min 38 s older than the response Date header (23:39:19Z), consistent with the docs' "refreshed every 10 minutes". That says nothing about odds age.
3. Even with a key, the vendor documents that its age stamp does not prove price age. The PS3838 Swagger text says every event carries updatedAt, "the time the feed last wrote that document. The scraper rewrites every event it still tracks on each pass, so read it as a freshness stamp for the document rather than as the moment a price last moved."
4. The stream protocol never sends updatedAt, markets[].updatedAt or oddsSig ("Never sent, never diffed"), and the vendor's Python client drops them (_IGNORED_TOP and _IGNORED_MARKET). The delta frame's "ts" can only show PulseScore-to-client delay.
5. The pass interval of the scraper is not stated anywhere I read.
6. I found no third-party latency measurement, Reddit or HN thread, GitHub issue or Trustpilot page. The sportsapis.dev review says its ratings come from "directory research" (not hands-on tests), and its connection and rate figures for ULTRA are out of date.

verdict.why:
This is an advertisement for PulseScore, not a method.

The free tier cannot be rapid. It is REST only, 500 requests a month, with no socket and no stream. The article's own WebSocket example fails on the free key it tells readers to use.

The cheapest live push is PRO at €79 a month, which is above the cheap line. STARTER at €20 is REST at 1 request/min per bookmaker, so it is worse than CNO.

The data is scraped, and the vendor says so. The age of any price is unprovable. The only freshness stamp, updatedAt, is rewritten on every scrape pass and the vendor says it is not the moment a price moved. The stream strips it out entirely. The vendor's best figure is a delta arriving 1-2 s after its own database write, "not a sub-second feed". The scrape-pass interval is never stated. That is the "real-time claim without a stated age" the bar calls worthless.

Coverage of what Vigilant needs is thin. Only PS3838 (likely Pinnacle's Asian brand), Kalshi and Polymarket overlap with the sharp list. Vigilant already reads Pinnacle (PinnWire/pinnapi), Kalshi and Polymarket directly, so PulseScore would be an extra hop over a scrape of them. It has no Circa, ProphetX, Sporttrade or Novig, and no documented player props. Hockey is not live at PS3838.

Scores are the book's own scoreboard and arrive no earlier than that book's price. They cannot beat Sofascore at 2.5 s, or Polymarket's socket, ahead of Novig's 16 s re-quote. That last point is INFERRED.

The delta-stream design (snapshot, keyed patches, seq, resume) is a sound pattern, but Vigilant's existing push sources already do the same job.

In short, it is unmeasured and probably not ahead of the sources Vigilant already has. Treat it as a €79-a-month, unmeasured, scraped second copy of Pinnacle. Only a 7-day PRO trial plus a free-key comparison could change that, and the free-key test below should settle it first.

result.what_it_is: The page is a templated "How to Scrape Odds Shark" recipe (difficulty 4/5, 60 min) on Scraperly, which calls itself "an independent web scraping reference database" covering 683+ sites. Scraperly is not a service: its About page says "Scraperly is not a proxy company or a scraping-as-a-service provider." The recipe gives no endpoint, no proxy settings and no real code. Its only commands are an `npm install claude-code` line, a garbled `mkdir` line, and `npx claude-code --task "Launch Puppeteer to load Odds Shark NFL page and extract current moneylines and spreads"`. Its only output is a one-line example JSON of NFL moneylines and spreads. It says the endpoint and proxy details are omitted and tells the reader to use an official API or authorized access and to stop on any 403 or challenge. The companion page https://scraperly.com/scrape/odds-shark adds two generic code examples (requests+BeautifulSoup on the oddsshark.com homepage, and a Scrapy spider with ROBOTSTXT_OBEY) and says "Odds Shark serves mostly static HTML". The key finding is that the target no longer exists as a standalone odds site. Every oddsshark.com URL I tested returns an HTTP 301 to covers.com, so the recipe describes a site that has been absorbed into Covers.
result.upstream_data_source: Not found for OddsShark. Neither Scraperly, Covers nor any search result names an odds feed vendor. Covers' odds page says only "Odds are supplied by sportsbooks and are subject to a small delay", "Opening odds are from a reputable international sportsbook with the highest limits", and "Consensus numbers are powered by Covers Contests". Facts I did find. (1) oddsshark.com now redirects to Covers: `www.oddsshark.com/` goes to `covers.com/oddsshark#oddsshark`, `/nfl/odds` goes to `covers.com/sport/football/nfl/odds#oddsshark`, and `/nba/odds` goes to the NBA equivalent. covers.com/oddsshark says "Odds Shark is now part of Covers." (2) Covers' footer reads "Copyright © 1995 - 2026 Genius Sports", its ToS names "CS Media Limited", and news reports Genius Sports bought Legend (Covers.com, Casino.org, Casino Guru) for up to $1.2B, announced 5 Feb 2026 and closed 1 May 2026. The Wikipedia page on Covers says Covers "was included in a $1.2 billion acquisition by Genius Sports in February 2026". (3) The Covers odds page is server-rendered HTML with each price in a `<td class="liveOddsCell" data-book data-game data-type data-date>`. Each cell carries a betslip `lineId` and `sideId`, which suggests an internal line database. The CSP header on robots.txt allows `wss://*.covers.com` and `wss://*.nssmp.com/websocket`, but I did not find any odds-related socket in the page scripts I read. Who feeds that database (a Genius/Betgenius product, scrapers of each book, or deep-link affiliate feeds) is unproven. The nine books shown are all US soft books.
result.push_or_poll: Poll only, and the poll is a full-page GET. Covers' NFL odds page is rendered on the server at load. The page's own scripts that I read (odds-page.js and sport-bundle.js, 9 KB and 5 KB) contain no setInterval, WebSocket, EventSource or fetch loop. Their only network call is an $.ajax that swaps in HTML when you change the odds scope. Each page load is about 3.4 MB. There is no push channel to a client. I did not read the other scripts on the page (betslip.js, footer-include.js, AffScript.js).
result.claimed_latency_or_refresh: Scraperly (second-hand, undated, uncited): "Odds Shark implemented real-time line tracking in 2026, updating odds every 3 seconds across sportsbooks." Covers: "real-time betting lines" and "live betting odds for every league" (no interval given), plus "Odds are supplied by sportsbooks and are subject to a small delay." Marketing only; none of it is a measurement.
result.measured_or_verified_age: I made three GETs of https://www.covers.com/sport/football/nfl/odds on 2026-10-07. The page prints "Last updated <time> ET" to the minute. Compared with the HTTP Date header: fetch 1 had Date 23:40:13 UTC (7:40 PM ET) and stamp 7:38 PM, so the snapshot was about 2 min old. Fetch 2 had Date 23:43:17 and stamp 7:43 PM. Fetch 3 had Date 23:44:19 and stamp 7:44 PM. So the page snapshot was 0 to 2 min behind my request, and the stamp is mostly the render time, not a proof of when each price was seen. Fetch 1 lacked bet365 changes already stamped 23:38:15 and 23:39:15 that fetch 2 contained, so that snapshot really was at least 2 min behind the data. Each odds cell also has an undocumented `data-date` epoch. It is INFERRED to be the time that line last changed. In fetch 3 the youngest stamps were 65 s, 65 s, 65 s, 180 s and 217 s old and the median spread cell was about 12.7 h old. Changed stamps cluster on bet365 at :14 or :15 past the minute (23:38:15, 23:39:15, 23:43:14), which hints at roughly one-minute polling of that book. Six cells changed between fetches 1 and 2 (3 min apart) and four between 2 and 3. A 3-second refresh is not visible in any of this, and the page's own code has no refresh loop. For Vigilant, the usable age is a snapshot that is 0 to 2 min old, plus however old each book's own price is. I could not measure the age of the underlying book prices, because the site has no per-price "seen at" field, only a last-change time.

verdict.why: This source is a thin tutorial about a target that has since disappeared. The Scraperly recipe is generic, has no endpoint, and its "3 seconds" claim is uncited. Odds Shark itself now 301-redirects to covers.com. Covers' odds page is a server-rendered HTML snapshot with no refresh loop, and I measured it 0 to 2 minutes behind my own request, with price changes landing about a minute apart. Its nine columns are all US soft books (no Pinnacle, Circa, Kalshi, ProphetX, Sporttrade or Novig). The data carries no per-price age beyond an undocumented last-change stamp. That is at best the same age as CNO (13-33 s cadence plus 1-2 min of lag) and from less useful books, so it cannot beat CNO's fair price or Novig's makers (16 s after a play). It is not a score source. It is also free only in cash: ToS section 19 says "You agree not to access the Services by any means other than through the interface", and the owner is Genius Sports. result.upstream_data_source:
Not stated by the vendor. Two pieces of evidence point to a resold third-party feed.

1. VERIFIED text: the B2B openapi.json (altLines) says "Groups are normalized to `total` and `spread` (sport-specific OpticOdds markets are mapped under those names)". INFERRED from that: the odds are a hop on OpticOdds, which is on the known list (SSE, sales-led).
2. The consumer app's GraphQL carries a per-line field named `odds_jam_run` next to `last_run`. INFERRED: OddsJam lineage, since the field name is the only evidence. I found no vendor statement of it.

The docs also refer to "producers" and a "first warm cycle", and the consumer help text says "when Surebetfusion last checked these bets". INFERRED, weakly: the pipeline is cyclic ingest, then normalize, then hub, rather than a book's own socket. Scores upstream: not found. The consumer app uses espncdn.com only for team-logo images, which does not mean ESPN is the score source.
result.push_or_poll:
The docs describe PUSH for main-market odds and scores. WebSocket hub `wss://events.surebetfusion.com` (auth message, then subscribe to channels like `odds/live/tennis/*` or `scores/live/soccer/*`). It sends change-only deltas with event_id, stream_id and a per-client sequence. Odds events are limited to moneyline, total and spread. Player props, alt lines and snapshots are POLL-only via `POST https://api.surebetfusion.com/graphql`, with a Bearer key and rate limits of 30 to 3,000 requests per minute by plan.

The marketing page's code tab shows a different transport: a GraphQL `onPriceChange` subscription at `wss://api.surebetfusion.com/graphql/realtime`. The docs say live data is NOT available via /graphql. The two pages disagree.

Consumer app (JS bundle): AppSync subscriptions `onLeagueUpdated` and `onScoresUpdated`, plus socket.io `live-score-update` events. The odds list refetches on a league notice at most once every 3 s (constant `Fz=3e3`), a UI throttle.

None. I measured nothing and found no third-party measurement, forum thread or GitHub issue about this product's latency.

What I could verify:
- No keyless data endpoint exists, so I could not compare a payload time to a Date header. Every data route needs a key: the GraphQL needs a Bearer key, and the WebSocket needs an auth message after "hello".
- The documented socket envelope `timestamp` is "Producer-hub emission time in Unix seconds". That is when the hub sent the event, not when the book's price was set, so it cannot prove the age of the underlying price.
- The documented B2B GraphQL line fields are only `id sportsbook price decimalPrice`. There is no per-line updated-at or last-checked field in the B2B API.
- The consumer app's internal GraphQL does have per-line `last_run` and `odds_jam_run`. The UI formats it as seconds, minutes or hours ("Ns/Nm/Nh") from epoch seconds. That timestamp is not in the documented B2B schema.
- The home-page "214 ms" and "3,184 updates/s" readouts are random: site.js sets `latency = 180 + Math.round(Math.random()*90)` and `live = 2600 + Math.round(Math.random()*1400)` every 1.1 s, and the ticker prices are a random walk of plus or minus 5. They are decoration, not measurements.

verdict.why:
ODDS: not a cheap or free rapid source.
- The free sandbox has no live odds, only pre-match.
- The cheapest paid tier with a live odds socket is Pro at $399/mo, and the docs say it is delayed 30 seconds, which is no better than CNO's 13-33 s cadence.
- "Real-time" odds start at Growth, $799/mo. That is CLAIM_ONLY and has no usable timestamp. The socket timestamp is hub emission time, and the B2B lines carry no per-line age field.
- The socket gives main markets only and caps the book list at 10 even on Growth.
- The upstream is a repackaged feed, apparently OpticOdds (INFERRED from the docs' wording). That is already on the known list as sales-led and SSE, so this adds a hop and its own 30 s throttle rather than a fresher source.
- The headline numbers (214 ms, 3,184 updates/s) are random numbers generated in the page's JavaScript. The "sub-second on every paid plan" table row is contradicted by the vendor's own pricing and docs.
- Compared with known sources: Polymarket's CLOB socket and Kalshi are free and push. The Odds API, ParlayAPI and PropLine are also cheaper. SportsGameOdds (from $49 a month) and TheRundown (Ultra, $399 for WebSocket) are cheaper or equal for the same kind of claim.
- No terms are published, and there is no stated right to bet automatically on the data.

SCORES: the only live lead.
- The docs describe a push scores channel (`scores/live/{sport}`) with no 30 s delay, and the plan table has a sandbox row.
- Unresolved: (a) whether the free key has the `live` scope (the docs call the entry tier "Starter", which the pricing page does not list); (b) what the score source is; (c) how old a score is when the hub emits it.
- If it exists it is a free key plus a socket. But the presets only mention tennis and soccer, and the bar is a lead of 3 s or more before Novig's re-quote (median 16 s). Sofascore REST at 2.5 s already shows a 15-27 s median lead, so this must beat Sofascore to matter.
- Prior: a vendor hub fed by cyclic producers is unlikely to beat Sofascore polling, but nobody has measured it.

TECHNIQUE: the subscribe, buffer, then snapshot handoff with per-client sequence plus event_id dedupe is sound, but Vigilant already does the equivalent on its Polymarket sockets. Nothing to port.

verdict.why: This is a how-to for scraping slow, public odds-comparison sites, not a data source. It names no feed with a timestamp, no real socket, and no sharp book. Its three targets (OddsPortal, BetExplorer, Flashscore) are one company's sites. Their best claim is a 15-second page refresh, but some books are read only once per minute or per 7 minutes. That is not ahead of CNO's 13-33 s cadence plus its 1-2 minute lag, and nowhere near Novig makers, who re-quote about 16 s after a play. Their age indicator has 10-minute resolution, so a price's age can never be proven. Scraping them would break Livesport's terms (automated requests, 'scraping', 'aggregating', commercial use) and robots.txt. Proxies, stealth and CAPTCHA tips solve a problem a phone polling a few public JSON feeds does not have. Browser automation does not suit an Android app. The only useful technique is DevTools hunting for the XHR or WebSocket a public site already uses (the Network tab's WS filter shows the socket URL and frame format), and that only helps on a site whose terms allow it. The article's one verified, relevant fact (Pinnacle's public API closed 23 Jul 2025, and its odds endpoints are limited to 1 request per 2 minutes per sport even for approved users) matches what the project already knows. Proxy cost is low, but there is nothing worth buying proxies for here.

It has an Express + ws server, an in-memory betting service with a fake R$ 1,000 wallet, and a zero-build browser page. Its "odds engine" is a SIMULATION: a timer that random-walks made-up prices and fakes goals and baskets. It does not read any real odds or scores. Commits are authored "claude", on a branch named like a Claude Code web session branch (claude/betting-app-websocket-EVVNt). Read 2026-10-07.
result.upstream_data_source: None. There is no upstream feed at all. The prices come from `server/engine.js` (header comment: "applying a simulation step"), seeded from 7 invented fixtures in `server/data.js` and moved by Math.random(). I know this because: (1) the server code has no outbound HTTP/fetch/API-key/env usage except PORT (grep of all server files; the only fetch() calls are the browser calling its own /api/bets); (2) package.json dependencies are only express, ws and nanoid; (3) the README says "an odds simulation engine". The seeded events (Flamengo v Palmeiras, Lakers v Celtics, Alcaraz v Sinner) are fiction, not mirrored from any real match.
result.push_or_poll: Push. The server holds a WebSocket at ws://host/stream?userId=... and sends a `snapshot` on connect, then an `updates` message every tick, plus `event:finished`, `balance` and `bet:settled`. Plain REST (GET /api/events, POST /api/bets) sits alongside it. There is no SSE and no queue; the "pipeline" is a Node EventEmitter inside one process. The browser reconnects with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s ... capped at 30s, no jitter). The server pings every 30 s and drops sockets that miss a pong.
result.claimed_latency_or_refresh: README: "every ~1.5s the engine ticks and pushes deltas to all connected clients". Code: `TICK_MS = 1500`, `SUSPEND_MS = 4000` (markets lock 4 s after a fake goal). This is the demo's own timer cadence, not the age of any real price.
result.measured_or_verified_age: None. There is no real price to age. Every price is generated server-side at tick time, and the event object carries no per-price timestamp (only startTime and suspendedUntil). Even for its own fake data the client could not tell how old a price is. Nothing here could meet the bar of a price "with a TIMESTAMP that proves its age".
result.coverage: No real coverage. Fiction only: 7 seeded events across soccer (Brasileirao, Premier League, La Liga), basketball ("NBA") and tennis ("ATP Masters"). Markets are match winner, totals (2.5 goals / 210.5 points), both-teams-to-score and total sets, in decimal odds with Portuguese labels. There are no US sports in the sense Vigilant needs (no NFL/MLB/NHL/college), no player props, no real books (no Pinnacle/Circa/Kalshi/ProphetX/Sporttrade/Novig), and no real in-play odds or live scores. verdict.why: This is not a source of anything. The repo is a two-commit, zero-star, unlicensed, untested demo (25 May 2026, authored by a Claude session) whose odds and scores are invented by Math.random() on a 1.5 s timer. It has no upstream feed, no real books, no US sports and no timestamps. 'Free' applies only to reading the code, since there is no data to be free. It cannot be ahead of CNO (13-33 s plus 1-2 min lag) or of Novig's makers (16 s median after ESPN's stamp), because it carries no information about the real world. Nothing in it competes with the known sources (Polymarket socket, Kalshi, Sofascore REST, ESPN, statsapi, PinnWire, etc.). Patterns worth copying into a Kotlin client, none of which is new or needs this repo: (1) snapshot-then-updates with full snapshot replay on every reconnect, so the client never reconciles partial state (Vigilant's Polymarket and Kalshi sockets should already work this way); (2) heartbeat plus capped exponential backoff (on the phone, OkHttp pingInterval; add jitter, which this demo lacks); (3) expectedPrice sent with each order and rejected with the live newPrice if it moved by more than a threshold, which is the same idea as Vigilant refusing to take a stale bid; (4) a market 'suspension window' after a score event (their 4 s lock), which Vigilant could mirror by treating the moments after a score as 'do not post or take', given Novig's makers re-quote ~5-16 s later; (5) engine and betting service decoupled through events. Demo-only parts to ignore: the whole price model and its hand-picked shock constants, the sped-up clocks, the in-memory wallet, the lack of auth, and the README's 'deltas' (the code sends whole events every tick). A real gap to avoid: no per-price timestamp and no client stale watchdog, the exact thing Tj's bar demands. In Vigilant, every pushed price should carry its source timestamp, and the feed should show 'age since last message' with a watchdog.

The technique, a WebSocket relay of scraped bookmaker boards, is nothing new for a phone app. The API itself is a possible odds source but nothing about its speed is proven. ODDS: the vendor's own best statement is a 1-2 s delay after its own write and 'not a sub-second feed', and the scraper's pass interval is never stated, so the real age of a PS3838 or DraftKings price is unknown. Only REST and legacy-WS events carry `updatedAt`, a document write stamp that the vendor says is not the moment a price moved. The Stream API sends no age field at all. If the scraper revisits live boards every few seconds it could beat CNO's 13-33 s cadence plus its 1-2 min lag. That is unmeasured, and I could not read a data response without a key. The incremental value is also small, because Vigilant already has Pinnacle (PinnWire/pinnapi), Kalshi and Polymarket directly and free. PulseScore's Kalshi and Polymarket are an extra hop over those, and its other books are mostly retail US books scraped through a third party. COST: free is 500 requests a month on REST only (a test budget, not a feed). STARTER €20 allows 1 request a minute per book, which is no faster than CNO. A socket needs PRO at €79 a month, well above Tj's $5 ParlayAPI scale and the under-50 bar. SCORES: no. Scores are each book's own board score, relayed after the book shows it, with no independent score source. They are not earlier than Sofascore REST at 2.5 s, Polymarket's score socket or ESPN. TERMS/RISK: no automated-use ban and no ban on betting use was found, but there is a no-resale clause, a disclaimer of real-time accuracy, and a scraped upstream that a book could cut off. The pricing page contradicts the docs on whether the free plan has a socket. Treat it as unproven and low priority. Run one free-tier REST test (below) and drop it if updatedAt ages are over about 5 s.

result.what_it_is: PulseScore is a young (blog posts from Feb-Mar 2026, Stream API live "since mid-September", terms updated 2026-10-07) paid REST + WebSocket API. It re-serves odds, scores and match clocks that it scrapes from 58 bookmakers' public sites in one normalized JSON schema. Its own homepage says "scraped from top bookmakers". It started as a Bet365 odds API (Product Hunt maker: Emil Mitev; the terms name no legal entity, only a gmail contact). It carries no licensed or official data. Scores are only whatever each book's own board shows, and some books are odds-only.
result.upstream_data_source: The vendor's own scraper reading the bookmakers' public boards. Not a licensed feed, and not a reseller of another API vendor. How I know: (1) homepage 2026-10-08: "Live betting odds from soccer and tennis - scraped from top bookmakers and updated every second"; (2) PS3838 Swagger spec at api.pulsescore.net/api/ps3838/doc: "The scraper rewrites every event it still tracks on each pass"; (3) Terms s.1 "aggregated publicly available sports betting odds data", s.6 "aggregates odds data from third-party bookmaker sources"; (4) results are a "live-mirror" of the book's in-play board ("last score and match clock the book published"). PS3838 is a Pinnacle-family brand by second-hand reports; Kalshi odds are "derived from the last traded price plus the current best bid/ask", so they are not the raw order book. The scrape cycle time is not stated anywhere.
result.push_or_poll: Both, but push needs a paid plan. REST polling (X-Secret header): 1 req/s per bookmaker on BASIC and PRO, 1 req/min on STARTER, 3/s on MAX, 6/s on ULTRA, 15/s absolute cap per key. Push (PRO or higher only, per the docs): (a) legacy wss://api.pulsescore.net/api/{book}/ws/live?key=..&sport=.. sends a full snapshot of every live event for the sport about once a second; (b) the beta Stream API, wss://api.pulsescore.net/api/stream/ws, sends one snapshot, then delta frames batched once per second per stream. Both push at 1 Hz, so the server itself quantizes to 1 s. Inference: PRO's REST limit of 1 req/s per book matches the socket's 1 frame/s, so the socket saves requests but adds no speed.
result.claimed_latency_or_refresh: Marketing: "Live in-play betting odds refreshed every ~1 second" (homepage), "one frame every second". Product Hunt maker: goal of "under 1 second" live and pre-match refresh "up to 60 seconds" (stated as goals, not results). Most candid vendor statement, in the Stream API docs: "a delta typically arrives 1-2 seconds after the bookmaker's write; this is not a sub-second feed". It is ambiguous whether "bookmaker's write" means the book's change or PulseScore's database write for that book. No percentiles, no benchmark, no scrape-interval figure anywhere.
result.measured_or_verified_age: None measured. A keyed payload could not be read (no sign-up, no key), so payload time versus Date header was not compared. What is verified: (1) Only the PS3838 spec documents a per-event updatedAt, defined as "the time the feed last wrote that document... a freshness stamp for the document rather than as the moment a price last moved". It is therefore a scrape-pass time and understates price age. I found the same field documented for no other book. (2) The Stream API docs say updatedAt, markets[].updatedAt and oddsSig are "never sent". (3) The legacy socket frame's `timestamp` (epoch ms) and the stream delta's `ts` (undefined in the docs) have no documented meaning as data age. So for the socket feeds, the age of a price cannot be proven from the response. The public capabilities JSON (Date 2026-10-08 00:02:36 GMT, discoveredAt 55 s earlier) is metadata, not odds.

result.price_and_free_tier: Read 2026-10-08. BASIC free: 500 requests/month, 1 req/s per bookmaker, all bookmakers, results, deep links. STARTER EUR 20/mo: 30,000 requests/month, 1 req/min per bookmaker. PRO EUR 79/mo (7-day free trial, monthly billing only): unlimited requests, 1 req/s per bookmaker, 1 live socket per bookmaker, Stream API 1 connection and 1 sport. MAX EUR 149/mo: 3 req/s, 3 sockets, Stream API 2 connections and 3 sports. ULTRA EUR 249/mo: 6 req/s, 6 sockets, Stream API 3 connections and all sports. 6-month plans cost 5 months (EUR 395 for PRO), 12-month plans cost 9 months (EUR 711 for PRO). Free-tier sockets: the pricing and home pages list "Live WebSocket connections" and "Stream API (delta streams)" under BASIC and STARTER. The docs rate table says "WebSocket None", the docs connection-limits table says "0 (REST only)", and the PS3838, Kalshi and DraftKings specs say "BASIC and STARTER plans are rejected with close code 4003". The stream docs say it is for PRO, MAX and ULTRA only and that other plans get HTTP 402. A dev.to article by PulseScore (Apr 10) and a third-party review also say no sockets on Basic and Starter. So the free tier is REST only, and 500 requests last about 8 minutes at 1 req/s. The only plan with a push socket and no per-minute REST cap is PRO at EUR 79.

"Attempt to circumvent rate limits, authentication, or any security measures." s.4: "Regardless of plan, an absolute maximum of 15 requests per second per API key applies to all API usage." s.6: "we make no guarantees regarding real-time accuracy, completeness, or availability... You use the data entirely at your own risk." s.2: paid plans are non-refundable once any API call has been made, with a 24-hour refund window only if no call was made. s.3: the 7-day trial is PRO monthly only, and plans auto-renew. s.7: they can terminate without notice. verdict.why: Odds: PulseScore is a scraper-reseller. Its fastest honest figure is that the socket batches at 1 Hz and a delta arrives 1-2 s after a write that is never defined. It publishes no scrape-cycle time and no price-age stamp. The one updatedAt, on PS3838, is a scrape-pass stamp that understates price age, and the socket and stream feeds omit it. So 'fresher than CNO's 13-33 s plus 1-2 min lag' is plausible if the claim holds, but nothing proves it, and a book's price scraped at 1 Hz cannot beat a direct socket. Cheapness: the free plan (500 requests/month, REST only, sockets rejected with 4003 despite the pricing page) covers about 8 minutes of 1 req/s polling. STARTER at EUR 20 is capped at 1 req/min per book, slower than CNO. Only PRO at EUR 79/mo gives 1 req/s per book plus a socket, which is above the under-50 bar. Versus the known sources: Kalshi and Polymarket odds are free and direct, and PulseScore's Kalshi is derived from last trade, so worse. The only candidate edge is Pinnacle-family prices via PS3838 for NFL/NBA/MLB/tennis live, with no live hockey, and no Circa, ProphetX, Sporttrade or Novig. Scores: this relays each book's own board, only where the book offers one. It is not an independent score source and has no evidence of leading Sofascore's free 2.5 s REST poll, which showed 22 of 29 Novig-moving scores 3 s or more early. Use in Vigilant: technically easy (keyed JSON and WebSocket). It is worth it only if a short free-tier measurement shows PS3838 data aged under about 3 s; otherwise no. The ToS and key-on-device caveats apply.

result.corrected_verdict:
usable_in_vigilant = no (unchanged from the scout). BkSignal cannot become a free or cheap part of Vigilant, for these reasons.

ODDS: none of the 22 books is a sharp or US book, so they cannot anchor a Novig fair price. The books are Russian/CIS/European retail and crypto casinos, with main markets only, no props and no baseball. The age of a price is never provable, because the only timestamp is BkSignal's own updated_at.

SCORES: this is the one thing worth thinking about, and it is unproven and probably structurally too coarse. The schema has no in-game tennis point. The score block is optional ('Not always'). The free test endpoint (2 events, 1 call per 30 s) is slower than the Novig re-quote it would have to beat, so it cannot measure a lead. Sofascore REST at 2.5 s already holds the measured result (median 6.4 s ahead of Polymarket's socket, 22 of 29 Novig-moving scores >= 3 s early), so BkSignal adds nothing known to exist.

COST: $5 per line looks cheap, but the real cost is the fixed-IP relay VPS the IP-bound key requires, a crypto payment (INFERRED), and your time. The 2-event free trial still needs an account.

TERMS: there are none. Nothing forbids betting use or automation, and nothing grants rights to the data either. robots.txt allows all. Tj has already chosen to ignore CNO's no-bots terms, so the missing terms are not what disqualifies it. Fit is. The things a skeptic should flag are a sole anonymous operator with a personal Telegram contact, no SLA, no licence, likely unlicensed scraped upstreams (INFERRED; the project forbids scraping bookmakers' consumer APIs itself), and sanctions/payment-compliance exposure that I did not research.

WHAT SURVIVES: a speculative $5 Fonbet-tennis probe through a fixed-IP relay, only if Tj wants to close the question. It is not worth building toward. 'Technique-only' gives nothing either, because an updateVersion cursor for incremental polling is a generic pattern.

Corrections to the scout:
- bksignal.com redirects (302) to odds.bksignal.com rather than serving the same page, and its body names a Telegram notifier bot and a personal contact.
- The register form's first field is 'login' and the Telegram field is optional.
- 'No NFL/college' is unverifiable, because 'Football' is undefined.
- The Cyrillic names are in the volleyball example, not football.
- ip_locked may mean rebind after a 1-minute cooldown.

result.corrected_verdict: Not a rapid odds or score source for Vigilant at free or cheap cost. Same bottom line as the scout, with corrections. (1) Free: false. BASIC is REST only, 500 requests a month, no socket, no stream; the article's own WebSocket snippet fails on the free key (close code 4003). (2) Cheap: false. The first push plan is PRO at EUR 79 a month; STARTER (EUR 20) polls at 1 request a minute per bookmaker. (3) Rapid: unproven. The odds are scraped from consumer bookmaker sites, the stream is batched once a second, and the vendor's own docs say a delta arrives 1-2 s after 'the bookmaker's write' and is 'not a sub-second feed'. 'The bookmaker's write' is undefined, the scrape-pass interval is stated nowhere, and the only freshness stamp (updatedAt) is a document-rewrite time that the Stream API drops. The article's '1 second / ahead of the curve' is marketing with no stated age. (4) The scout's dismissals that need softening: PS3838 live ice hockey is offered (liveSportsOffered and the Swagger live keys), the capabilities live list rotates; the pricing page claims player props on every plan (CLAIM_ONLY, undocumented per book); US retail books could in principle feed a consensus; the score inference is sound against PS3838's own price but whether it leads Novig's re-quote is simply unmeasured. (5) What remains true: only PS3838 (likely Pinnacle's Asian brand, INFERRED), Kalshi and Polymarket overlap Vigilant's sharp list, and Vigilant already reads those directly, so PulseScore is a second scraped hop. Scores are the book's own scoreboard and cannot beat Sofascore at 2.5 s (INFERRED). Only a free-key REST spot check (about 10 of 500 requests, done by Tj) followed by a PRO trial test against Vigilant's direct Pinnacle and Kalshi reads could change this. The test would need a median lead of at least 3 s, and even then it costs EUR 79 a month.

details.free_tier_limits: VERIFIED (https://pulsescore.net/terms section 4 and pricing page, read 2026-10-08): BASIC is free, 500 requests a month, 1 request/s per bookmaker, REST only. Live WebSocket and Stream API are crossed out on the card; the docs table says 'BASIC 0 (REST only)'. The pricing page lists 'Live in-play odds' as 'same on every plan', so live REST polling works on BASIC but is capped at about 16 requests a day. Absolute cap of 15 requests/s per key on every plan.
details.websocket_or_live_included_free: No. PRO and above only (PRO 1 socket per bookmaker or 1 stream connection for 1 sport; MAX 3 per bookmaker; ULTRA 6). The docs' close code 4003 means plan too low. Live in-play odds exist over REST on the free key, but it is not a push, and the stream page says the stream copy is 'byte-for-byte what the REST API would return', so REST polling at 1 request/s per bookmaker (PRO and up; unlimited requests) would give the same state as the socket.

Capabilities 2026-10-08T00:14Z: PS3838 live american-football, baseball, basketball, soccer, tennis at that moment, with ice-hockey, esports and rugby-league in liveSportsOffered; Kalshi live includes american-football, baseball, basketball, cricket, esports, ice-hockey, soccer, tennis, volleyball; FanDuel and DraftKings live include american-football, baseball, basketball, ice-hockey, soccer, tennis. The pricing page claims 'Full market boards including player props' (CLAIM_ONLY); no US-book prop market appears in any Swagger text I read; sportsapis.dev says no props.
details.sharp_books_or_exchanges_covered: Of Vigilant's sharp list: PS3838 (likely Pinnacle's Asian brand, INFERRED; the vendor never says Pinnacle), Kalshi (prices derived from last trade plus best bid/ask, per its Swagger), Polymarket. Not present: Circa, ProphetX, Sporttrade, Novig. Others on the list of 58: Betfair exchange liquidity under orbitxch, BetOnline, Bovada and Cloudbet, plus many EU and AU books. None of these carries a documented price age.
details.duplicates_what_the_app_already_has: Largely yes. PS3838, Kalshi and Polymarket are already read directly (PinnWire/pinnapi, Kalshi, Polymarket sockets); PulseScore would be a scraped second hop with batching on top (INFERRED). The only new input would be US retail books (FanDuel, DraftKings, BetMGM, BetRivers, Hard Rock, Bet365 etc.) as a possible fresh consensus, which is plausible in principle and unmeasured.
details.signup_friction: BASIC: sign up on pulsescore.net and generate a key in the dashboard; the vendor says no credit card is required (marketing, not tested here; I did not sign up). It would have to be Tj's own account. PRO: 7-day free trial, monthly billing only; whether a card is required is not stated on the pricing page or terms. Terms section 2: paid plans non-refundable once any API call is made.
details.terms_of_use: VERIFIED (https://pulsescore.net/terms, Last updated October 7, 2026): no resale, redistribution or sublicensing without written consent; no scraping or systematic extraction of the API beyond the plan's intended usage; no circumventing rate limits; no 'facilitate illegal gambling operations'. Access can be cut at any time (section 7). Section 6 disclaims real-time accuracy, completeness and availability; section 9 excludes lost profits. Upstream legal and continuity risk (consumer bookmakers' own terms, Cloudflare and endpoint changes that the vendor's 2026-07-04 post says break scrapers) sits with the vendor.
details.betting_use_or_automated_use_allowed: Nothing in the terms forbids using the data to place your own bets or running it from an app; resale or sharing to other users is forbidden. Stay inside the plan's rate limit (ten 429s within ten seconds pauses a key for 60 s, per the scout; not re-verified by me). A single phone key also runs into the per-bookmaker socket cap (extra connections replace the oldest with close code 4012).
details.android_phone_feasibility: Technically easy: plain HTTPS with an X-Secret header plus gzip, or a WSS socket (wss://api.pulsescore.net/api/{bookmaker}/ws/live?key=..&sport=.. sends one frame about every second with every live event for that sport). The Stream API defaults to live plus prematch, and a full prematch soccer snapshot can be 20-450 MB, so a client would have to declare kinds=live. Sockets are per account, so phone and any other client share the cap. Feasible, but the data's age and the EUR 79 price are the blockers, not the plumbing. The key must stay out of the public repo.
